ScientistTwo: Pioneering the Human
Knowledge Frontier with Autonomous AI
Jaehyun Nam1, Jinsung Yoon1, Yanzhou Pan1, Yubo Wang2, Rui Meng1, Parthasarathy Ranganathan1 and
Tomas Pfister1
1Google Cloud AI Research, 2University of Waterloo
Scientific discovery is defined by the ability to identify the boundaries of existing knowledge and
venture into unexplored territory. The ultimate vision for AI in science is problem-driven autonomous
research: given a fundamental challenge by a human expert, the AI independently navigates the scientific
landscape, uncovers theoretical and empirical bottlenecks, and systematically expands the frontier of
knowledge. In this paper, we introduce ScientistTwo, a fully autonomous multi-agent framework designed
to realize this vision. Specifically, ScientistTwo takes an initial problem as input, establishes state-of-
the-art baselines, formulates novel hypotheses, and coordinates specialized agents to orchestrate an
end-to-end discovery cycle without human intervention. Moreover, the framework rigorously conducts
experiments using diverse datasets and metrics, refines methodologies through automated ablation
studies, and validates research findings via a closed-loop simulated peer-review rebuttal engine. To
evaluate ScientistTwo’s capabilities against the highest standards of human scientific achievement, we
benchmark it across papers accepted at top-tier conferences such as ICLR, ICML, and NeurIPS. As a result,
ScientistTwo autonomously generates expert-level, publishable papers and fully verified, executable
codebases. Its solutions consistently outperform human state-of-the-art models, and achieve higher
average review ratings than human-authored papers under automated AI review agents. These results
show that ScientistTwo is not merely an assistive tool but an autonomous scientific pioneer capable of
pushing the frontiers of human discovery. Project website: https://scientist-two.github.io/
1. Introduction
Scientific discovery has long been the hallmark of human ingenuity, defined by the ability to identify
the boundaries of current knowledge and venture into the unknown. With the rapid advancement of
foundation models (Liu et al., 2024; Singh et al., 2025; Team et al., 2023), artificial intelligence (AI)
is transitioning from a passive conversational assistant to an active participant in the scientific process
(Jansen et al., 2025; Meng et al., 2026; Xu and Peng, 2025). The ultimate ambition of this paradigm
is purely problem-driven autonomous discovery: a human researcher simply specifies a scientific
challenge, and an autonomous AI independently navigates the landscape of human knowledge,
diagnoses theoretical and empirical bottlenecks, formulates novel hypotheses, and executes the
end-to-end research lifecycle on its own to pioneer the human knowledge frontier.
Despite recent progress in the field of autonomous research agents (Tang et al., 2026a; Weng et al.,
2025; Yamada et al., 2025), a substantial gap remains between automated assistant systems and
rigorous empirical scientific standards. Existing systems primarily focus on optimizing single-scalar
metrics on isolated benchmarks, lacking the multi-dimensional reasoning capabilities required to
tackle complex scientific problems (Chen et al., 2026c; Jin et al., 2026). More importantly, current
agents lack the closed-loop empirical rigor of human scientists who continuously iterate based on
evidence. They cannot systematically conduct ablation studies to isolate causal mechanisms for
improvement, nor can they engage in dynamic peer-review processes essential for validating ideas
and addressing methodological critiques through targeted supplementary experiments.
Corresponding author(s): jaehyunnam@google.com, jinsungyoon@google.com

Figure 1 | Teaser. ScientistTwo pushes the frontier of human knowledge across diverse research
domains (e.g., LLMs, robotics, neuroscience, speech, robustness, reinforcement learning, game theory,
privacy, optimization, and time series) by generating publication-quality papers and fully verified
codebases, with the resulting methodologies consistently outperforming human state-of-the-art
baselines. Specifically, ScientistTwo improves 86 out of 107 papers (an 80.4% success rate) with an
average relative improvement of 25.2% over human state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, papers
generated by ScientistTwo surpass the average scores of accepted papers at ICLR 2026 and NeurIPS
2025 under the Stanford Agentic Reviewer, demonstrating its capability to produce manuscripts that
reach the empirical acceptance standards of top-tier AI venues.
To overcome these fundamental challenges, we introduce ScientistTwo, an expert-level autonomous
multi-agent framework designed to pioneer the frontier of human knowledge (see Figure 1). Specif-
ically, ScientistTwo operates on a foundational division of labor: the human researcher defines
the target scientific challenge, while the AI autonomously orchestrates the path to advance it. To
rigorously demonstrate this capability against the highest standard of scientific rigor, we subject
ScientistTwo to the real-world testing ground: given competitive peer-reviewed human research from
top-tier AI venues (e.g., ICLR, ICML, NeurIPS), ScientistTwo must independently discover meaningful
advancements beyond the established state-of-the-art, while simultaneously demonstrating that its
autonomous scientific discovery process is measurable, reproducible, and transparent.
To achieve expert-level rigor across diverse disciplines demanded by top-tier science, Scien-
tistTwo coordinates a collaborative ecosystem of specialized agents (see Figure 3):
• Holistic Benchmark Reasoning & Efficient Screening: Rather than overfitting to a single metric,
ScientistTwo evaluates proposed ideas across comprehensive, multi-dataset benchmarks. To
balance computation efficiency, it employs a subset-first evaluation strategy, rapidly filtering
ideas on representative benchmark slices before allocating compute to full-scale experiments.

VD-STRANS: ULTRA-LOW-LATENCY INCREMENTAL
BYTE PAIR ENCODING
VIA VECTORIZED DIRECT-
INTERVAL SUFFIX TRANSDUCTION
Anonymous authors
Paper under double-blind review
ABSTRACT
Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) subword tokenization is a foundational computational
primitive in large language model (LLM) pipelines, yet its dynamic greedy pri-
ority heap maintenance and pointer-chasing search tree traversals present signiﬁ-
cant throughput bottlenecks in streaming inference and massive data preprocess-
ing. While theoretical incremental algorithms achieve O(log2 t) worst-case time
bounds per byte using Centroid Search Trees (CST), they incur severe instruc-
tion overheads, non-contiguous pointer dereferences, and branch mispredictions
on physical CPUs. In this work, we present Vectorized Direct-Interval Suf-
ﬁx Transducer (VD-STrans), an ultra-low-latency incremental BPE framework.
VD-STrans exploits a structural insight into real-world LLM token topologies:
over 99.1% to 99.8% of all Sufﬁx-Successor Trees SufSucTree(ω) in production
vocabularies contain at most 8 nodes. VD-STrans ﬂattens these compact tree
topologies into 256-bit aligned Compact Flat Decision Vectors (FDVs) and re-
solves candidate last-token selection via a branchless 256-bit AVX2 SIMD parallel
range comparison kernel in O(1) cycle time. Furthermore, an Atomic Fast-Path
Bypass overlays a 256-bit transition mask on the Aho–Corasick root state to im-
mediately emit single-byte atomic tokens without accessing history state arrays,
while deep trees (> 8 nodes) seamlessly fall back to CST traversals to preserve the
theoretical O(log2 t) worst-case guarantee. Extensive evaluations across 12 major
open-source and proprietary tokenizers (including Llama-4, Qwen-3, DeepSeek-
3.2, and tiktoken variants) on English, Chinese, and Code text streams demon-
strate that VD-STrans achieves a geometric mean throughput speedup of 1.123→
over state-of-the-art incremental BPE (with peak speedups of 1.271→) and up to
23.64→over standard heap-based BPE, while maintaining 100% exact tokeniza-
tion ﬁdelity.
1
INTRODUCTION
Subword tokenization is an essential preprocessing step in modern large language model (LLM)
pipelines, serving as the bridge between raw character streams and discrete token representations
(Sennrich et al., 2015; Dubey et al., 2024). As neural architectures and attention computations
have been dramatically accelerated through IO-aware implementations such as FlashAttention (Dao
et al., 2022), text preprocessing operations—traditionally regarded as minor administrative over-
heads—increasingly emerge as signiﬁcant latency bottlenecks in real-time inference, streaming text
generation, and massive data ingestion pipelines.
Among various subword segmentation schemes, Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) (Sennrich et al., 2015)
remains the de facto standard due to its deterministic greedy merge logic and effective vocabulary
compression, alongside probabilistic alternatives such as Unigram language modeling (Kudo, 2018;
Bostrom & Durrett, 2020) and regularized variants like BPE-dropout (Provilkov et al., 2019). Stan-
dard ofﬂine BPE tokenizers (e.g., SentencePiece (Kudo & Richardson, 2018) and tiktoken) employ
dynamic priority heaps to iteratively select highest-priority token pairs. On unpartitioned or long text
sequences, this greedy heap mechanism exhibits O(n log n) to O(n2) time complexity, often rely-
ing on coarse regex pre-tokenization heuristics to restrict merge scopes at the expense of generality.

Theoretical investigations into BPE have established that optimal compression via pair encoding is
APX-complete (Kozma & Voderholzer, 2024), reinforcing the reliance on heuristic merge structures.
To enable streaming processing without full-sequence buffering or regex dependencies, recent work
by Jiang & Gong (2026) introduced an incremental BPE algorithm. By formalizing the Preﬁx Con-
sistency property (Berglund & van der Merwe, 2023) and introducing Sufﬁx-Successor Trees and
Centroid Search Trees (CST), this approach incrementally updates the valid tokenization preﬁx in
O(log2 t) worst-case time per byte, supported by fast Aho–Corasick state tracking (Kanda et al.,
2022).
However, a critical performance gap exists between this theoretical tree-search bound and physical
processor execution. Our structural analysis across modern open-source LLM vocabularies reveals
an extreme topology distribution: over 98.6% to 99.8% of all Sufﬁx-Successor Trees SufSucTree(ω)
contain at most 8 nodes, with an average tree depth of only 2 to 3 nodes. Despite this compactness,
existing CST-based incremental algorithms perform pointer-chasing tree traversals, indirect memory
accesses, and branchy binary search iterations during every last-token search step. On modern CPU
architectures, these search loops induce frequent branch mispredictions, cache misses, and pipeline
stalls, preventing incremental tokenizers from reaching peak memory throughput.
To resolve these computational inefﬁciencies, we propose the Vectorized Direct-Interval Sufﬁx
Transducer (VD-STrans), an ultra-low-latency incremental BPE framework that replaces explicit
search tree traversals with branchless SIMD parallel range evaluation and atomic fast-path bypass-
ing. VD-STrans introduces three core technical innovations:
1. Compact Flat Decision Vectors (FDV): For every canonical token whose Sufﬁx-
Successor Tree contains 8 or fewer nodes (→8), VD-STrans ﬂattens the hierarchical
tree topology into a contiguous memory layout storing candidate token IDs, sufﬁx history
offsets |suc(ti)|, and Depth-First Search (DFS) pre-order entry/exit interval timestamps
[Lti, Rti).
2. Branchless SIMD Parallel Interval Range Kernel: Rather than executing iterative tree
searches or binary loops, VD-STrans fetches history timestamps dfsin(H(|sc| ↑|suc(ti)|))
for all candidates simultaneously and evaluates interval membership [Lti, Rti) in paral-
lel using a single 256-bit AVX2 SIMD vector comparison ( mm256 cmpgt epi32 and
mm256 and si256). A bitmask extraction ( mm256 movemask ps) and trailing-zero-
count instruction (tzcnt) identify the exact valid last token ε(sc) in O(1) branchless
execution time.
3. Atomic Fast-Path Bypass & Hybrid CST Fallback: VD-STrans incorporates a 256-
bit transition bitmask on the Aho–Corasick root node to immediately output single-byte
atomic tokens when no multi-byte sufﬁx extensions exist, bypassing history state array
maintenance entirely. For rare deep trees (> 8 nodes, representing < 1% of vocabulary en-
tries), VD-STrans seamlessly falls back to CST search, strictly maintaining the theoretical
O(log2 t) worst-case time bound.
We evaluate VD-STrans across 12 diverse LLM tokenizers (including Llama 3.1, Qwen-3,
DeepSeek-3.2, and OpenAI tiktoken encodings) and real-world datasets spanning English, Chinese,
and Code text domains. Across all 72 evaluated benchmark conﬁgurations, VD-STrans achieves
a geometric mean speedup of 1.123↓over the state-of-the-art CST incremental algorithm (with
peak speedups up to 1.271↓) and up to 23.64↓over standard ofﬂine heap implementations on non-
pretokenized text streams, while guaranteeing 100% byte-identical tokenization accuracy and robust
worst-case stability. While the state-of-the-art CST baseline already captured the primary algorith-
mic gains over naive priority heaps, VD-STrans eliminates the remaining physical CPU execution
bottlenecks—yielding a vital 12.3% average throughput boost (and up to 27.1% peak) that directly
translates into hardware infrastructure savings for streaming inference serving.
2

Subword tokenization and ofﬂine BPE.
Subword tokenization is a foundational component
of modern NLP pipelines (Sennrich et al., 2015; Kudo, 2018; Bostrom & Durrett, 2020). Byte
Pair Encoding (BPE), adapted from dictionary compression (Gall´e, 2019), iteratively merges the
most frequent adjacent pairs into vocabulary entries. Practical implementations—Hugging Face

tokenizers, SentencePiece (Kudo & Richardson, 2018), and OpenAI tiktoken—employ dy-
namic priority heaps and rely on regex pre-tokenization (Dagan et al., 2024) to keep heap operations
from scaling quadratically. Recent theory formalizes tokenization structurally: Geng et al. (2024)
model byte BPE as an inverse string homomorphism, and Cognetta & Okazaki (2024) compile
subword algorithms into ﬁnite-state transducers. To accelerate batch pretraining, BlockBPE (You,
2025) executes concurrent intra-block merges on GPUs; however, these ofﬂine frameworks require
buffering blocks or re-tokenizing preﬁxes from scratch, making them ill-suited to streaming text.
Incremental tokenization and search-tree structures.
Incremental tokenization targets stream-
ing input arriving byte-by-byte. Its theoretical basis is the Preﬁx Consistency property (Berglund
& van der Merwe, 2023): truncating a valid BPE token sequence yields a valid tokenization of the
corresponding preﬁx. Building on this, Berglund et al. (2024) study DFA constructions for BPE
transduction and Mamouras et al. (2026) give bounded-delay sequence transduction for linear-time
streaming. To maintain exact standard BPE semantics without delay bounds or regex partition-
ing, Jiang & Gong (2026) introduced an incremental BPE algorithm over Aho–Corasick automata
(Kanda et al., 2022) and Sufﬁx-Successor Trees, applying Centroid Decomposition (Gagie et al.,
2013) to precompute Centroid Search Trees (CST) with an O(log2 t) per-byte bound. Yet CST
traversals incur heavy pointer-chasing on modern CPUs. VD-STrans resolves this by observing that
> 99% of Sufﬁx-Successor Trees are small (→8 nodes), replacing pointer searches with branchless
vector comparisons over ﬂat arrays.
Hardware-accelerated string processing and SIMD.
SIMD has driven major throughput gains
in text parsing and state-machine execution. In document parsing, simdjson (Langdale & Lemire,
2019) and Mison (Li et al., 2017) replace FSM control ﬂow with SIMD structural indexing and bit-
mask operations, eliminating branch mispredictions at multi-GB/s. For comparison-based search,
Khuong & Morin (2015) show that contiguous, cache-aligned layouts with branchless vector instruc-
tions outperform pointer-based trees for small sets (N →16). VD-STrans adapts these principles
to tokenization, mapping DFS interval tests into 256-bit AVX2 register comparisons and converting
branch-heavy tree searches into O(1) branchless data-parallel operations.
3
METHODOLOGY
In this section, we present the mathematical and structural framework of Vectorized Direct-Interval
Sufﬁx Transduction (VD-STrans). We ﬁrst review the formal topological foundations of incremental
Byte Pair Encoding (BPE), deﬁne the Preﬁx Last-Token Condition and Depth-First Search (DFS)
linearization, and then detail our high-performance hardware vectorization scheme, atomic fast-path
bypass, and hybrid centroid search fallback.
3.1
STRUCTURAL FOUNDATIONS OF INCREMENTAL BPE
Let ! be a ﬁnite byte alphabet, and let V ↑!+ denote a ﬁnite subword vocabulary consisting of
atomic tokens (|t| = 1) and non-atomic tokens (|t| > 1). A merge dictionary D = [r1, r2, . . . , rm]

Vocabulary Normalization and Successor Forest.
To eliminate non-canonical redundancies, we
normalize V such that every token t ↑V satisﬁes TD(t) = [t]. For non-atomic t, determinism yields
a unique canonical rule (x, y) ↓t, establishing predecessor pre(t) = x and successor suc(t) = y.
The Successor Forest Fsuc = (V, E) is a directed acyclic graph with edges E = {(u, suc(u)) | u ↑
V, |u| > 1} directed toward successors. Because length strictly decreases (|suc(u)| < |u|), Fsuc
forms a set of trees rooted at atomic character tokens.
Sufﬁx-Successor Tree.
For any canonical token ε ↑V , the Sufﬁx-Successor Tree, denoted as
SufSucTree(ε), is the subgraph of Fsuc induced by all canonical tokens that form sufﬁxes of ε.
Because all candidate sufﬁx tokens of sc share the same ﬁnal character c, SufSucTree(ε(sc)) forms
a uniﬁed tree structure rooted at atomic token c, where ε(sc) is the longest canonical sufﬁx token
recognized by an Aho–Corasick automaton maintained over V .
Preﬁx Last-Token Condition and Monotonic Path Property.
To determine whether a node t ↑
SufSucTree(ε(sc)) represents the exact last token ω(sc), t must satisfy structural reachability and
priority dominance constraints.
Deﬁnition 1 (Preﬁx Last-Token Condition). For string s and sufﬁx token t ↑V , t satisﬁes the Preﬁx
Last-Token Condition if t is atomic, or if t is non-atomic and for preﬁx state k = ω(s ↔suc(t)):
1. Reachability: k lies within the subtree of Fsuc rooted at pre(t) (including k = pre(t)).
2. Priority Dominance: If k ↗= pre(t), let u be the child of pre(t) on the ancestor path to k.
The canonical rule of t has strictly higher priority rank than u.
Theorem 1 (Monotonic Path Property (Jiang & Gong, 2026)). Let k = ε(sc) be the longest canon-
ical sufﬁx token of string sc. The set of nodes in SufSucTree(k) satisfying the Preﬁx Last-Token
Condition forms a unique contiguous path P starting from the atomic root c to ω(sc).

3.2
COMPACT FLAT DECISION VECTOR (FDV) FORMULATION
Existing incremental BPE implementations resolve the valid last token ω(sc) by performing Centroid
Decomposition search traversals over SufSucTree(ε), which incurs dynamic pointer dereferences,
non-contiguous memory accesses, and binary search branch loops.
Our empirical proﬁling across 12 modern LLM vocabularies reveals an extreme topological prop-
erty: over 99.1% to 99.8% of all Sufﬁx-Successor Trees contain at most 8 nodes, with average
tree depth ranging from 2.8 to 3.2. Inspired by this structural compactness, VD-STrans replaces
explicit pointer-based tree structures with Compact Flat Decision Vectors (FDVs).
For every canonical token ε where |SufSucTree(ε)| ↓8, we ﬂatten its tree topology in reverse
topological order (deepest candidate tokens ﬁrst) into a contiguous 256-bit SIMD-aligned memory
vector structure. An FDV entry packs candidate attributes into parallel arrays:

Unrolled Scalar Gather vs.
Native Vector Gather.
In Stage 1, non-contiguous history
timestamps are retrieved into vector registers.
While hardware vector gather instructions
( mm256 i32gather epi32) exist, microarchitectural benchmarking across Intel (Ice Lake,
Sapphire Rapids) and AMD (Zen 3, Zen 4) processors reveals that native gather instructions in-
cur high instruction latencies (12–20 clock cycles) due to internal microcode serialization and L1
memory port contention. In contrast, an unrolled scalar load loop into a 32-byte cache-aligned
temporary buffer followed by a single contiguous vector load ( mm256 load si256) executes in
only 5–7 cycles for N = 8 lanes, completely avoiding microcode sequencing stalls (see detailed
microarchitectural breakdown in Appendix B).
3.4
ATOMIC FAST-PATH BYPASS AND HYBRID CST FALLBACK
Atomic Fast-Path Bypass.
When processing raw text streams, character transitions frequently
land on single-byte atomic tokens that possess no multi-byte sufﬁx extensions in V . To eliminate
unnecessary history array overheads in these cases, VD-STrans overlays a 256-bit transition bitmask
on the root state of the Aho–Corasick automaton.
If the incoming byte transition c matches a root state with no sufﬁx extensions, the atomic bypass
ﬂag triggers immediately. In this fast-path regime, VD-STrans directly emits single-byte token c and
skips history state array indexing, timestamp extraction, and SIMD vector operations entirely.
Hybrid CST Fallback.
For rare deep Sufﬁx-Successor Trees where |SufSucTree(ε)| > 8 (repre-
senting < 0.8% of vocabulary entries), ﬂat SIMD register capacity is exceeded. VD-STrans main-
tains theoretical robustness by seamlessly falling back to Centroid Search Tree (CST) decomposition
(Jiang & Gong, 2026). This hybrid control ﬂow preserves the optimal O(log2 t) worst-case per-byte
time complexity, ensuring asymptotic stability on pathological or adversarial inputs.

We systematically
varied the tree ﬂattening cutoff threshold K ↔{0, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32} across representative tokenizers.
As shown in Fig. 3a, vocabulary coverage increases rapidly from 0% at K = 0 to 99.192% at

over Inc-orig). At K = 16 and K = 32, despite marginal coverage gains (99.88% and 99.97%),

a 1.074→geomean speedup, while dual 128-bit passes cover 99.2%—strong evidence for cross-
platform portability to ARM Neon targets (e.g., AWS Graviton and mobile processors).

lanes.
Ablation 4: Atomic Fast-Path Bypass Across Text Domains.
We evaluated the Atomic Fast-
Path Bypass across text domains with varying character entropy. Fast-path hit rates (percentage
of character transitions bypassing history lookups) were measured at 19.6%–23.3% on English,
19.7%–28.4% on Code, and 35.1%–98.0% on Chinese text.
On Chinese text with CodeLlama (98.0% fast-path hit rate), the atomic bypass yields a peak through-
put gain of 1.192→(geomean 1.103→across Chinese). Fast-path throughput gain exhibits a strong
positive correlation with hit rate (Pearson r = 0.811).
Ablation 5: Deep-Tree Fallback Strategy Analysis.
To evaluate fallback mechanisms for trees
exceeding 8 nodes, we stress-tested Centroid Search Tree (CST), Chained Multi-Vector SIMD, and
Linear Unrolled Scalar Search on synthetic trees with a forced 97% fallback rate across depths
m ↑[16, 255] (Fig. 3b). Linear scans achieve higher throughput for shallow trees (m ↓64) but
degrade linearly with depth, whereas CST maintains logarithmic stability (O(log2 m)) and crosses
over at m ↔96 nodes. This conﬁrms CST as the optimal fallback for preserving the O(log2 t)
worst-case bound on pathological inputs (e.g., a2k).
5
CONCLUSION
We introduced Vectorized Direct-Interval Sufﬁx Transducer (VD-STrans), an ultra-low-latency
incremental BPE framework.
Exploiting the structural observation that > 99.1% of Sufﬁx-
Successor Trees in real-world LLM vocabularies contain ↓8 nodes, VD-STrans ﬂattens dynamic
tree topologies into 256-bit aligned Compact Flat Decision Vectors and resolves last-token selection
through a branchless AVX2 SIMD range kernel, an Atomic Fast-Path Bypass, and a CST fallback
for deep trees—eliminating pointer dereferences, branch mispredictions, and search-loop overheads.
Across 12 tokenizers and 3 text domains, VD-STrans attains a geometric-mean speedup of 1.123→
(up to 1.271→) over the state-of-the-art incremental algorithm and up to 23.64→over heap baselines,
with 100% exact ﬁdelity. Limitations and future work. VD-STrans is tuned for 256-bit AVX2, but
our K=4 topology analysis shows strong potential for 128-bit ARM Neon; porting the vectorized
primitives to ARM Neon and RISC-V Vector for edge deployment, and extending direct-interval
transduction to hardware-accelerated FPGA/GPU preprocessing, are promising directions.

relative improvement over the human-designed state-of-the-art baseline (Jiang and Gong, 2026).
Moreover, evaluated under the ICLR peer-review procedures, this AI-authored paper is accepted,
receiving impressive scores of 8.0 from ScholarPeer and 6.5 from the Stanford Agentic Reviewer.
• Ablation-Driven Hypothesis Refinement: Emulating the empirical rigor of expert researchers, Sci-
entistTwo autonomously designs and executes ablation studies to isolate individual component
contributions, dynamically pruning ineffective components and refining its core hypothesis.
• Dynamic Peer-Review & Rebuttal Loops: To ensure publication-grade validity, generated drafts
are critiqued by a simulated Peer-Review Agent. Rather than treating review comments as
passive editorial guidance, a dedicated Rebuttal Agent actively conceives, codes, and executes
targeted supplementary experiments to address critique. A Meta-Review Agent oversees this
cycle, triggering recursive refinement loops until rigorous acceptance criteria are satisfied.
We evaluate ScientistTwo across 107 diverse research challenges encompassing diverse areas
such as optimization, reinforcement learning, large language models (LLMs), and theory (see Fig-
ure 1). Specifically, ScientistTwo successfully advances 80.4% of the target problems, delivering
an average relative performance gain of 25.2% over the original human state-of-the-art baselines.
Furthermore, the autonomously generated manuscripts and executable codebases consistently achieve
high acceptance rates across independent automated peer-review evaluations with high scores. These
results demonstrate that ScientistTwo moves beyond passive empirical problem-solving, serving as an
autonomous pioneer capable of systematically expanding the frontiers of scientific knowledge.

relative improvement over the human-designed state-of-the-art baseline (Jiang and Gong, 2026).
Moreover, evaluated under the ICLR peer-review procedures, this AI-authored paper is accepted,
receiving impressive scores of 8.0 from ScholarPeer and 6.5 from the Stanford Agentic Reviewer.


  • Ablation-Driven Hypothesis Refinement: Emulating the empirical rigor of expert researchers, Sci-
     entistTwo autonomously designs and executes ablation studies to isolate individual component
      contributions, dynamically pruning ineffective components and refining its core hypothesis.
  • Dynamic Peer-Review & Rebuttal Loops: To ensure publication-grade validity, generated drafts
     are critiqued by a simulated Peer-Review Agent. Rather than treating review comments as
      passive editorial guidance, a dedicated Rebuttal Agent actively conceives, codes, and executes
     targeted supplementary experiments to address critique. A Meta-Review Agent oversees this
      cycle, triggering recursive refinement loops until rigorous acceptance criteria are satisfied.


  We evaluate ScientistTwo across 107 diverse research challenges encompassing diverse areas
such as optimization, reinforcement learning, large language models (LLMs), and theory (see Fig-
ure 1). Specifically, ScientistTwo successfully advances 80.4% of the target problems, delivering
an average relative performance gain of 25.2% over the original human state-of-the-art baselines.
Furthermore, the autonomously generated manuscripts and executable codebases consistently achieve
high acceptance rates across independent automated peer-review evaluations with high scores. These
results demonstrate that ScientistTwo moves beyond passive empirical problem-solving, serving as an
autonomous pioneer capable of systematically expanding the frontiers of scientific knowledge.

BYTE PAIR ENCODING
VIA VECTORIZED DIRECT-

Anonymous authors
Paper under double-blind review

Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) subword tokenization is a foundational computational
primitive in large language model (LLM) pipelines, yet its dynamic greedy pri-
ority heap maintenance and pointer-chasing search tree traversals present signiﬁ-
cant throughput bottlenecks in streaming inference and massive data preprocess-
ing. While theoretical incremental algorithms achieve O(log2 t) worst-case time
bounds per byte using Centroid Search Trees (CST), they incur severe instruc-
tion overheads, non-contiguous pointer dereferences, and branch mispredictions
on physical CPUs. In this work, we present Vectorized Direct-Interval Suf-
ﬁx Transducer (VD-STrans), an ultra-low-latency incremental BPE framework.
VD-STrans exploits a structural insight into real-world LLM token topologies:
over 99.1% to 99.8% of all Sufﬁx-Successor Trees SufSucTree(ω) in production
vocabularies contain at most 8 nodes. VD-STrans ﬂattens these compact tree
topologies into 256-bit aligned Compact Flat Decision Vectors (FDVs) and re-
solves candidate last-token selection via a branchless 256-bit AVX2 SIMD parallel
range comparison kernel in O(1) cycle time. Furthermore, an Atomic Fast-Path
Bypass overlays a 256-bit transition mask on the Aho–Corasick root state to im-
mediately emit single-byte atomic tokens without accessing history state arrays,
while deep trees (> 8 nodes) seamlessly fall back to CST traversals to preserve the

Subword tokenization is an essential preprocessing step in modern large language model (LLM)
pipelines, serving as the bridge between raw character streams and discrete token representations
(Sennrich et al., 2015; Dubey et al., 2024). As neural architectures and attention computations
have been dramatically accelerated through IO-aware implementations such as FlashAttention (Dao
et al., 2022), text preprocessing operations—traditionally regarded as minor administrative over-
heads—increasingly emerge as signiﬁcant latency bottlenecks in real-time inference, streaming text
generation, and massive data ingestion pipelines.

Among various subword segmentation schemes, Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) (Sennrich et al., 2015)
remains the de facto standard due to its deterministic greedy merge logic and effective vocabulary
compression, alongside probabilistic alternatives such as Unigram language modeling (Kudo, 2018;
Bostrom & Durrett, 2020) and regularized variants like BPE-dropout (Provilkov et al., 2019). Stan-
dard ofﬂine BPE tokenizers (e.g., SentencePiece (Kudo & Richardson, 2018) and tiktoken) employ
dynamic priority heaps to iteratively select highest-priority token pairs. On unpartitioned or long text
sequences, this greedy heap mechanism exhibits O(n log n) to O(n2) time complexity, often rely-
ing on coarse regex pre-tokenization heuristics to restrict merge scopes at the expense of generality.
Under review as a conference paper at ICLR 2025

Theoretical investigations into BPE have established that optimal compression via pair encoding is
APX-complete (Kozma & Voderholzer, 2024), reinforcing the reliance on heuristic merge structures.

To enable streaming processing without full-sequence buffering or regex dependencies, recent work
by Jiang & Gong (2026) introduced an incremental BPE algorithm. By formalizing the Preﬁx Con-
sistency property (Berglund & van der Merwe, 2023) and introducing Sufﬁx-Successor Trees and
Centroid Search Trees (CST), this approach incrementally updates the valid tokenization preﬁx in
O(log2 t) worst-case time per byte, supported by fast Aho–Corasick state tracking (Kanda et al.,
2022).

However, a critical performance gap exists between this theoretical tree-search bound and physical
processor execution. Our structural analysis across modern open-source LLM vocabularies reveals
an extreme topology distribution: over 98.6% to 99.8% of all Sufﬁx-Successor Trees SufSucTree(ω)
contain at most 8 nodes, with an average tree depth of only 2 to 3 nodes. Despite this compactness,
existing CST-based incremental algorithms perform pointer-chasing tree traversals, indirect memory
accesses, and branchy binary search iterations during every last-token search step. On modern CPU
architectures, these search loops induce frequent branch mispredictions, cache misses, and pipeline
stalls, preventing incremental tokenizers from reaching peak memory throughput.

To resolve these computational inefﬁciencies, we propose the Vectorized Direct-Interval Sufﬁx
Transducer (VD-STrans), an ultra-low-latency incremental BPE framework that replaces explicit
search tree traversals with branchless SIMD parallel range evaluation and atomic fast-path bypass-
ing. VD-STrans introduces three core technical innovations:
1. Compact Flat Decision Vectors (FDV): For every canonical token whose Sufﬁx-

Successor Tree contains 8 or fewer nodes (→8), VD-STrans ﬂattens the hierarchical
tree topology into a contiguous memory layout storing candidate token IDs, sufﬁx history
offsets |suc(ti)|, and Depth-First Search (DFS) pre-order entry/exit interval timestamps
[Lti, Rti).
2. Branchless SIMD Parallel Interval Range Kernel: Rather than executing iterative tree

searches or binary loops, VD-STrans fetches history timestamps dfsin(H(|sc| ↑|suc(ti)|))
for all candidates simultaneously and evaluates interval membership [Lti, Rti) in paral-
lel using a single 256-bit AVX2 SIMD vector comparison ( mm256 cmpgt epi32 and
mm256 and si256). A bitmask extraction ( mm256 movemask ps) and trailing-zero-
count instruction (tzcnt) identify the exact valid last token ε(sc) in O(1) branchless
execution time.
3. Atomic Fast-Path Bypass & Hybrid CST Fallback: VD-STrans incorporates a 256-

bit transition bitmask on the Aho–Corasick root node to immediately output single-byte
atomic tokens when no multi-byte sufﬁx extensions exist, bypassing history state array
maintenance entirely. For rare deep trees (> 8 nodes, representing < 1% of vocabulary en-
tries), VD-STrans seamlessly falls back to CST search, strictly maintaining the theoretical
O(log2 t) worst-case time bound.

We evaluate VD-STrans across 12 diverse LLM tokenizers (including Llama 3.1, Qwen-3,
DeepSeek-3.2, and OpenAI tiktoken encodings) and real-world datasets spanning English, Chinese,
and Code text domains. Across all 72 evaluated benchmark conﬁgurations, VD-STrans achieves
a geometric mean speedup of 1.123↓over the state-of-the-art CST incremental algorithm (with
peak speedups up to 1.271↓) and up to 23.64↓over standard ofﬂine heap implementations on non-
pretokenized text streams, while guaranteeing 100% byte-identical tokenization accuracy and robust
worst-case stability. While the state-of-the-art CST baseline already captured the primary algorith-
mic gains over naive priority heaps, VD-STrans eliminates the remaining physical CPU execution
bottlenecks—yielding a vital 12.3% average throughput boost (and up to 27.1% peak) that directly
translates into hardware infrastructure savings for streaming inference serving.

Subword tokenization and ofﬂine BPE.
Subword tokenization is a foundational component
of modern NLP pipelines (Sennrich et al., 2015; Kudo, 2018; Bostrom & Durrett, 2020). Byte
Pair Encoding (BPE), adapted from dictionary compression (Gall´e, 2019), iteratively merges the
most frequent adjacent pairs into vocabulary entries. Practical implementations—Hugging Face
Under review as a conference paper at ICLR 2025

tokenizers, SentencePiece (Kudo & Richardson, 2018), and OpenAI tiktoken—employ dy-
namic priority heaps and rely on regex pre-tokenization (Dagan et al., 2024) to keep heap operations
from scaling quadratically. Recent theory formalizes tokenization structurally: Geng et al. (2024)
model byte BPE as an inverse string homomorphism, and Cognetta & Okazaki (2024) compile
subword algorithms into ﬁnite-state transducers. To accelerate batch pretraining, BlockBPE (You,
2025) executes concurrent intra-block merges on GPUs; however, these ofﬂine frameworks require
buffering blocks or re-tokenizing preﬁxes from scratch, making them ill-suited to streaming text.

Incremental tokenization and search-tree structures.
Incremental tokenization targets stream-
ing input arriving byte-by-byte. Its theoretical basis is the Preﬁx Consistency property (Berglund
& van der Merwe, 2023): truncating a valid BPE token sequence yields a valid tokenization of the
corresponding preﬁx. Building on this, Berglund et al. (2024) study DFA constructions for BPE
transduction and Mamouras et al. (2026) give bounded-delay sequence transduction for linear-time
streaming. To maintain exact standard BPE semantics without delay bounds or regex partition-
ing, Jiang & Gong (2026) introduced an incremental BPE algorithm over Aho–Corasick automata
(Kanda et al., 2022) and Sufﬁx-Successor Trees, applying Centroid Decomposition (Gagie et al.,
2013) to precompute Centroid Search Trees (CST) with an O(log2 t) per-byte bound. Yet CST
traversals incur heavy pointer-chasing on modern CPUs. VD-STrans resolves this by observing that
> 99% of Sufﬁx-Successor Trees are small (→8 nodes), replacing pointer searches with branchless
vector comparisons over ﬂat arrays.

Hardware-accelerated string processing and SIMD.
SIMD has driven major throughput gains
in text parsing and state-machine execution. In document parsing, simdjson (Langdale & Lemire,
2019) and Mison (Li et al., 2017) replace FSM control ﬂow with SIMD structural indexing and bit-
mask operations, eliminating branch mispredictions at multi-GB/s. For comparison-based search,
Khuong & Morin (2015) show that contiguous, cache-aligned layouts with branchless vector instruc-
tions outperform pointer-based trees for small sets (N →16). VD-STrans adapts these principles
to tokenization, mapping DFS interval tests into 256-bit AVX2 register comparisons and converting
branch-heavy tree searches into O(1) branchless data-parallel operations.

Vocabulary Normalization and Successor Forest.
To eliminate non-canonical redundancies, we
normalize V such that every token t ↑V satisﬁes TD(t) = [t]. For non-atomic t, determinism yields
a unique canonical rule (x, y) ↓t, establishing predecessor pre(t) = x and successor suc(t) = y.
The Successor Forest Fsuc = (V, E) is a directed acyclic graph with edges E = {(u, suc(u)) | u ↑
V, |u| > 1} directed toward successors. Because length strictly decreases (|suc(u)| < |u|), Fsuc
forms a set of trees rooted at atomic character tokens.

Sufﬁx-Successor Tree.
For any canonical token ε ↑V , the Sufﬁx-Successor Tree, denoted as
SufSucTree(ε), is the subgraph of Fsuc induced by all canonical tokens that form sufﬁxes of ε.
Because all candidate sufﬁx tokens of sc share the same ﬁnal character c, SufSucTree(ε(sc)) forms
a uniﬁed tree structure rooted at atomic token c, where ε(sc) is the longest canonical sufﬁx token
recognized by an Aho–Corasick automaton maintained over V .

Preﬁx Last-Token Condition and Monotonic Path Property.
To determine whether a node t ↑
SufSucTree(ε(sc)) represents the exact last token ω(sc), t must satisfy structural reachability and
priority dominance constraints.
Deﬁnition 1 (Preﬁx Last-Token Condition). For string s and sufﬁx token t ↑V , t satisﬁes the Preﬁx
Last-Token Condition if t is atomic, or if t is non-atomic and for preﬁx state k = ω(s ↔suc(t)):

1. Reachability: k lies within the subtree of Fsuc rooted at pre(t) (including k = pre(t)).
2. Priority Dominance: If k ↗= pre(t), let u be the child of pre(t) on the ancestor path to k.

The canonical rule of t has strictly higher priority rank than u.
Theorem 1 (Monotonic Path Property (Jiang & Gong, 2026)). Let k = ε(sc) be the longest canon-
ical sufﬁx token of string sc. The set of nodes in SufSucTree(k) satisfying the Preﬁx Last-Token
Condition forms a unique contiguous path P starting from the atomic root c to ω(sc).

Unrolled Scalar Gather vs.
Native Vector Gather.
In Stage 1, non-contiguous history
timestamps are retrieved into vector registers.
While hardware vector gather instructions
( mm256 i32gather epi32) exist, microarchitectural benchmarking across Intel (Ice Lake,
Sapphire Rapids) and AMD (Zen 3, Zen 4) processors reveals that native gather instructions in-
cur high instruction latencies (12–20 clock cycles) due to internal microcode serialization and L1
memory port contention. In contrast, an unrolled scalar load loop into a 32-byte cache-aligned
temporary buffer followed by a single contiguous vector load ( mm256 load si256) executes in
only 5–7 cycles for N = 8 lanes, completely avoiding microcode sequencing stalls (see detailed
microarchitectural breakdown in Appendix B).

3.4
ATOMIC FAST-PATH BYPASS AND HYBRID CST FALLBACK

Atomic Fast-Path Bypass.
When processing raw text streams, character transitions frequently
land on single-byte atomic tokens that possess no multi-byte sufﬁx extensions in V . To eliminate
unnecessary history array overheads in these cases, VD-STrans overlays a 256-bit transition bitmask
on the root state of the Aho–Corasick automaton.

If the incoming byte transition c matches a root state with no sufﬁx extensions, the atomic bypass
ﬂag triggers immediately. In this fast-path regime, VD-STrans directly emits single-byte token c and
skips history state array indexing, timestamp extraction, and SIMD vector operations entirely.

Hybrid CST Fallback.
For rare deep Sufﬁx-Successor Trees where |SufSucTree(ε)| > 8 (repre-
senting < 0.8% of vocabulary entries), ﬂat SIMD register capacity is exceeded. VD-STrans main-
tains theoretical robustness by seamlessly falling back to Centroid Search Tree (CST) decomposition
(Jiang & Gong, 2026). This hybrid control ﬂow preserves the optimal O(log2 t) worst-case per-byte
time complexity, ensuring asymptotic stability on pathological or adversarial inputs.

robustness. AVX-512 offers no advantage over AVX2 (2.58 ns) because tree sizes rarely exceed 8
lanes.

Ablation 4: Atomic Fast-Path Bypass Across Text Domains.
We evaluated the Atomic Fast-
Path Bypass across text domains with varying character entropy. Fast-path hit rates (percentage
of character transitions bypassing history lookups) were measured at 19.6%–23.3% on English,
19.7%–28.4% on Code, and 35.1%–98.0% on Chinese text.

On Chinese text with CodeLlama (98.0% fast-path hit rate), the atomic bypass yields a peak through-
put gain of 1.192→(geomean 1.103→across Chinese). Fast-path throughput gain exhibits a strong
positive correlation with hit rate (Pearson r = 0.811).

Ablation 5: Deep-Tree Fallback Strategy Analysis.
To evaluate fallback mechanisms for trees
exceeding 8 nodes, we stress-tested Centroid Search Tree (CST), Chained Multi-Vector SIMD, and
Linear Unrolled Scalar Search on synthetic trees with a forced 97% fallback rate across depths
m ↑[16, 255] (Fig. 3b). Linear scans achieve higher throughput for shallow trees (m ↓64) but
degrade linearly with depth, whereas CST maintains logarithmic stability (O(log2 m)) and crosses
over at m ↔96 nodes. This conﬁrms CST as the optimal fallback for preserving the O(log2 t)
worst-case bound on pathological inputs (e.g., a2k).

We introduced Vectorized Direct-Interval Sufﬁx Transducer (VD-STrans), an ultra-low-latency
incremental BPE framework.
Exploiting the structural observation that > 99.1% of Sufﬁx-
Successor Trees in real-world LLM vocabularies contain ↓8 nodes, VD-STrans ﬂattens dynamic
tree topologies into 256-bit aligned Compact Flat Decision Vectors and resolves last-token selection
through a branchless AVX2 SIMD range kernel, an Atomic Fast-Path Bypass, and a CST fallback
for deep trees—eliminating pointer dereferences, branch mispredictions, and search-loop overheads.
Across 12 tokenizers and 3 text domains, VD-STrans attains a geometric-mean speedup of 1.123→
(up to 1.271→) over the state-of-the-art incremental algorithm and up to 23.64→over heap baselines,
with 100% exact ﬁdelity. Limitations and future work. VD-STrans is tuned for 256-bit AVX2, but
our K=4 topology analysis shows strong potential for 128-bit ARM Neon; porting the vectorized
primitives to ARM Neon and RISC-V Vector for edge deployment, and extending direct-interval
transduction to hardware-accelerated FPGA/GPU preprocessing, are promising directions.

high acceptance rates across independent automated peer-review evaluations with high scores. These
results demonstrate that ScientistTwo moves beyond passive empirical problem-solving, serving as an
autonomous pioneer capable of systematically expanding the frontiers of scientific knowledge.

et al., 2026a), and MARS (Chen et al., 2026c) automate end-to-end ML workflows by executing and
improving modeling pipelines, while data science agents such as DA-Agent (Huang et al., 2024), Data
Interpreter (Hong et al., 2025), and DS-STAR (Nam et al., 2026b) tackle heterogeneous data challenges
through structured planning and recursive verification. In this paper, we introduce ScientistTwo,
a specialized AI agent for autonomous research, from idea generation and implementation to the
writing of high-quality publishable academic papers.
Autonomous Research Agents. Autonomous research agents have rapidly evolved from ML problems
into sophisticated, multi-stage pipelines that coordinate the entire scientific workflow—from literature-
based analysis and hypothesis generation to execution and drafting of research papers. Early end-
to-end pipelines, such as AI Scientist (Lu et al., 2024), established this automation paradigm but
suffered from execution instability and issues with hallucinated writing; subsequent versions, such
as AI Scientist-v2 (Yamada et al., 2025), mitigated these problems through a best-first-tree search
for experimental branches and review-based reporting. At the same time, modular systems have
focused on resolving specific bottlenecks; for example, PaperOrchestra (Song et al., 2026) compiles
unconstrained experiment logs and ideas into LaTeX manuscripts, while ScholarPeer (Goyal et al.,
2026) deploys a multi-agent system that acts as peer-reviewers. Other frameworks introduce human-
in-the-loop gates (Schmidgall et al., 2025), apply evolutionary optimization to algorithmic discovery
(Lyu et al., 2026; Novikov et al., 2025), or focus on single-metric optimization for a target codebase
(Li et al., 2026d; Liu et al., 2026a; Tang et al., 2026a; Weng et al., 2025); however, they are generally
limited to optimizing a single scalar metric on a single dataset. Crucially, even verifiability-centric
systems like ScientistOne (Meng et al., 2026) lack the ability to perform an active analytical expansion.
Our ScientistTwo addresses these fundamental gaps by conducting systematic experiments on various
benchmark datasets and incorporating a dynamic peer-review loop, automating the iterative process
of performing complementary ablation experiments, refining ideas, and revising manuscripts, thus
producing expert-level papers that meet the rigorous standards of top academic venues.

ScientistTwo is an expert-level autonomous research agent that effectively orchestrates specialized AI
agents throughout the scientific discovery pipeline. First, ScientistTwo identifies the limitations of the
human state-of-the-art method regarding a given scientific problem and generates ideas to address

cumulative: modern progress relies on identifying the limitations of state-of-the-art work and develop-
ing methodologies to surpass them. To mirror this realistic research workflow, our goal is to build an
autonomous research agent A capable of executing continuous research iterations. Given a scientific
problem G, the framework generates a paper P+ paired with a reproducible codebase C+, which
represents new frontier knowledge on the given problem. Formally, we define this transformation as:

3.1. Generating Novel Seed Ideas: Targeting Limitation Resolution
Finding Limitations. ScientistTwo initiates the research pipeline by identifying the core limitations
of the human state-of-the-art method with respect to a given scientific problem G. Specifically, initially,
the Limitation Extractor extracts a set of limitations from G. Then, the Limitation Verifier verifies
whether this set is sufficient to guide novel improvements to G. If the Limitation Verifier considers
the set insufficient, the Limitation Extractor again identifies missing limitations or weaknesses and
expands the collection. This verification loop repeats until the Limitation Verifier confirms that all
actionable limitations have been thoroughly extracted or maximum number of iterations is reached.

3.4. Ablation Studies: Analyzing Source of Gain and Refining Ideas
Once the optimal candidate idea ℎbest is selected, ScientistTwo conducts systematic component-level
ablation studies. This phase isolates the explicit sources of empirical gain for scientific interpretation,
and leverages fine-grained ablation feedback to perform an additional round of idea refinement.
Ablation Planning and Execution. To evaluate individual components, an Ablation Planner Agent
automatically formulates a set of 𝑁𝑝executable ablation plans {𝑝1, . . . , 𝑝𝑁𝑝} tailored to ℎbest. For each
ablation plan 𝑝𝑖, an Ablation Coding Agent modifies the validated codebase Cbest to execute, yielding
an ablation outcome 𝑐𝑖. The aggregated ablation results are collected as Eabl = {𝑐1, . . . , 𝑐𝑁𝑝}.
Refining the Idea via Ablation Insights. Emulating expert human research practices, where removing
redundant or counterproductive components often yields a better method, ScientistTwo uses Eabl
to further refine ℎbest. An Ablation Critic Agent AAblCritic inspects the component breakdown to
determine whether ℎbest is optimal or requires additional modification, generating 𝑑abl, 𝑟abl where
𝑑abl ∈{Good, Refine}. If 𝑑abl = Good, ℎbest is finalized and passed to the paper drafting stage. If
𝑑abl = Refine, ScientistTwo re-engages the Full-Set Engineering Agent AFullEng to produce a refined
hypothesis ℎnew, updated results Enew, and revised codebase Cnew guided by critique 𝑟abl.
Robust Verification and Loop. Because structural refinements do not guarantee improved perfor-
mance, ScientistTwo verifies whether Enew strictly outperforms Ebest. The baseline variables are
updated—(ℎbest, Ebest, Cbest) ←(ℎnew, Enew, Cnew)—if and only if Enew is preferred than Ebest by the
Result Comparison Agent. When an update occurs, ScientistTwo re-executes the ablation planning
phase on the updated candidate. This refinement loop repeats for a maximum of 𝑁abl iterations or
until AAblCrit emits 𝑑abl = Good, ensuring a fully optimized hypothesis prior to manuscript generation.
3.5. Manuscript Drafting: Simulating the Peer-Review Process
Initial Drafting. First, an Initial Drafter Agent ADraft (incorporating PaperOrchestra; Song et al.,
2026) synthesizes the selected idea ℎbest, main benchmark results Ebest, and component ablation
studies Eabl into a full, conference-formatted manuscript Pnew.
Enhancing the Draft via Simulated Review-Rebuttal. To rigorously elevate manuscript quality, Sci-
entistTwo simulates an interactive peer-review and rebuttal process. A Peer-Reviewer Agent AReviewer
(i.e., ScholarPeer; Goyal et al., 2026) critically evaluates Pnew, generating a detailed evaluation
Rnew containing identified strengths, weaknesses, targeted questions, and an overall numerical score

entistTwo simulates an interactive peer-review and rebuttal process. A Peer-Reviewer Agent AReviewer
(i.e., ScholarPeer; Goyal et al., 2026) critically evaluates Pnew, generating a detailed evaluation
Rnew containing identified strengths, weaknesses, targeted questions, and an overall numerical score

4. Experiments
In this section, we empirically validate the effectiveness of ScientistTwo. Specifically, in § 4.1, we
present quantitative and qualitative comparisons against existing autonomous research agents. In
§ 4.2, we conduct component-wise ablation studies to evaluate each constituent part of ScientistTwo.
In § 4.3, we provide a discussion including cost analysis and case studies.
Common Setup. We evaluate the effectiveness of ScientistTwo on 107 scientific problems drawn from
top machine learning venues, including ICLR, ICML, and NeurIPS (see Appendix A.1 for details). All ex-
periments are conducted using Gemini 3.6 Flash and Claude Opus 4.8, unless otherwise specified. For
evaluation, we primarily report review scores from automated AI review agents: ScholarPeer (Goyal
et al., 2026) and Stanford Agentic Reviewer1. ScholarPeer serves as an in-distribution evaluation,
as it is also used to refine the draft quality generated by ScientistTwo. Conversely, Stanford Agentic
Reviewer serves as a held-out evaluator that was unseen during development by both the baselines
and our method. Full implementation details and configurations are provided in Appendix A.2.
4.1. Main Results
Quantitative Comparison. As shown in Table 2, ScientistTwo achieves a 91.9% acceptance rate under
ScholarPeer (nearly doubling the review score from ScientistOne’s 3.8 to 7.5). More importantly,
while all baselines fail to achieve acceptance from the Stanford Agentic Reviewer, ScientistTwo is the
only agent that produces research where 72.1% of generated papers meet high acceptance standards.
This result shows that while current autonomous research agents cannot produce expert-level research
results, ScientistTwo possesses such capabilities.
Qualitative Comparison. To assess the depth and completeness of the generated manuscripts, we
compare ScientistTwo against the strongest baseline, ScientistOne. As illustrated in Figure 8, Sci-
entistTwo demonstrates substantially broader experimental coverage and analytical rigor. While
ScientistOne generates only 4 figures and 2 tables—evaluating a single metric on an isolated bench-
mark with limited baselines—ScientistTwo produces 9 figures and 12 tables (including the Appendix).
Furthermore, ScientistTwo reports multi-metric evaluations across diverse datasets and incorporates
an extensive set of baseline comparisons, reflecting a publication-ready experimental design.

ScientistTwo: Pioneering the Human Knowledge Frontier with Autonomous AI
• Round-Robin Placement (C0): A naive baseline that assigns models sequentially across
available GPUs in a cyclic order, completely ignoring memory capacities and SLO require-
ments.
• OpenEvolve (C1): An automated discovery framework based on AlphaEvolve that utilizes
evolutionary search to ﬁnd optimal placement conﬁgurations [Brown et al., 2025].
• AdaEvolve: An adaptive, LLM-driven zeroth-order optimization approach that iteratively
reﬁnes placements based on performance feedback [Cemri et al., 2026].
• EvoX: The current state-of-the-art meta-evolutionary search framework for automated
discovery, as reported in the benchmark leaderboard.
Evaluation Metrics
For this task, a higher score indicates a superior, more balanced model
placement.
4.2
Main Results
The comparative performance of our proposed method against the baselines is summarized in Table 1.
Our Robust Multi-Heuristic Linearized Target Bisection method achieves a score of 26.2560. This
performance signiﬁcantly outperforms the naive Round-robin baseline, which completely fails to
optimize the objective, yielding a score of 0. Furthermore, our deterministic solver surpasses the
OpenEvolve framework, which achieves a score of 26.23.
Table 1: Comparison of model placement strategies on the Prism benchmark. The proposed method
provides a highly competitive, deterministic alternative to evolutionary search algorithms. Higher
scores indicate better KVPR minimization.

While our method demonstrates strong performance, we note that it is highly competitive with,
but slightly trailing, AdaEvolve (26.30) and falls short of the unconstrained meta-evolutionary
search employed by EvoX (30.52). However, this performance delta highlights a crucial trade-off
between placement quality and computational overhead. Methods like AdaEvolve and EvoX rely on
heavy, LLM-driven zeroth-order optimization and meta-evolutionary loops, which require substantial
compute and time to converge.
In contrast, our proposed method is entirely deterministic and mathematically grounded in fractional
bin-packing principles [Alvim et al., 2004]. It achieves a 100% success rate in ﬁnding feasible place-
ments with an exceptionally low execution time of approximately 0.021 seconds. By transforming
the non-linear KVPR objective into a linearized capacity constraint, our solver rapidly explores the
search space using standard 1D bin-packing heuristics [Fekete and Schepers, 2001], making it highly
suitable for dynamic, real-time cluster orchestration where millisecond-level scheduling latency is
required.
4.3
Ablation Studies
To understand the contribution of individual algorithmic design choices, we conducted an extensive
ablation study. We evaluated several mathematical relaxations and search strategies that were explored
during the development of our solver. The results of this ablation are detailed in Table 2.
Impact of Local Search Reﬁnement
Our core bisection search relies on sorting heuristics (e.g.,
First-Fit and Best-Fit descending) to ﬁnd feasible packings for a target KVPR. While highly effective,
heuristic bin-packing can occasionally leave small imbalances across GPUs. Removing the post-
bisection local search reﬁnement drops the score from 26.2560 to 26.2332. The local search phase

improvement over the standard Round-robin baseline.

systematically evaluates O(1) model moves and swaps from the bottleneck GPU. By incrementally
updating precomputed state arrays, this reﬁnement irons out residual heuristic imperfections without
inﬂating execution time, proving to be a critical "ﬁnisher" for the algorithm.
Linearization vs. Iterative Reassignment
We also explored alternative mathematical approaches
to handle the fractional KVPR objective. An Iterative Dinkelbach-style Reassignment approach
achieved a score of 26.1906, while a pure Fractional Optimization via Dinkelbach’s Iterative Lin-
earization scored 26.0157. Both approaches underperformed compared to our target bisection method.
The fractional nature of the objective W/(M →S) ↑K transforms perfectly into the linear constraint
W +K ·S ↑K ·M. Bisection over the target K allows the solver to leverage robust, globally-aware
bin-packing heuristics rather than relying on iterative, gradient-like reassignments that are prone to
local optima in heavily constrained spaces.
Failure of Clustering-Based Heuristics
Finally, we tested clustering-inspired heuristics, including
Lloyd-Max Iterative Reassignment (score: 25.9551) and Complementary Workload-Aware Model
Pairing (score: 25.8152). These methods attempt to balance the mean KVPR or pair complementary
models prior to placement. However, they consistently failed to tightly pack the 80GB bins compared
to capacity-linearized bisection. The strictness of the memory constraint dictates that optimizing
for capacity utilization is a prerequisite for optimizing the fractional objective; clustering methods
8

objective scores of various optimization formulations. The ﬁnal proposed method, Linearized Target
Bisection with Local Search Reﬁnement, achieves the highest score of 26.2560, demonstrating
its superiority over alternative mathematical relaxations such as Dinkelbach-style and Lloyd-Max
reassignment. The y-axis is truncated to highlight the ﬁne-grained performance differences between
the highly optimized variants.
inherently struggle to guarantee tight bin packings, leading to premature memory exhaustion and
sub-optimal maximum KVPR bounds.
5
Discussion and Conclusion
In this work, we addressed the critical challenge of minimizing Key-Value Cache Pressure (KVPR)
in multi-tenant Large Language Model (LLM) serving environments. By formulating the model
placement task as a strict non-linear fractional bin-packing problem, we introduced a deterministic,
three-phase algorithmic pipeline comprising greedy initialization, multi-heuristic linearized target
bisection, and local search reﬁnement. Our approach effectively transforms the non-linear KVPR
objective into a solvable 1D capacity constraint. Experimental results demonstrate that our method
achieves a highly competitive KVPR score of 26.2560, outperforming sophisticated meta-evolutionary
frameworks such as OpenEvolve [Brown et al., 2025] and AdaEvolve [Cemri et al., 2026] while
maintaining a negligible computational overhead of approximately 0.021 seconds.
Despite these strong empirical results, our approach has several limitations. First, our solver assumes
a static, upfront placement of models based on proﬁled request rates and Service Level Objectives
(SLOs). In highly dynamic production environments where workload patterns ﬂuctuate unpredictably,
static placement may eventually lead to suboptimal resource utilization. Unlike systems that employ
dynamic execution-level chunking [Agrawal et al., 2023] or live migration of KV cache states [He
et al., 2025], our method does not currently adapt to real-time trafﬁc shifts after the initial placement.
Second, our formulation assumes a uniform 80GB memory constraint across all GPUs. While this
reﬂects standard high-end accelerator deployments, it does not account for heterogeneous clusters
with mixed memory capacities or complex network topologies, which have been explored in recent
systems like Helix [Mei et al., 2024] and DisHelis [Zhang et al., 2026]. Finally, our model abstracts
GPU memory as a contiguous pool, relying on the assumption that underlying systems handle
memory fragmentation effectively through techniques like virtual memory stitching or dynamic
paging [Prabhu et al., 2024].
Future research should explore extending our linearized bisection framework to online, dynamic
serving scenarios. Integrating our placement algorithm with proactive live migration mechanisms
could allow the system to continuously rebalance KVPR as request rates deviate from initial estimates

4.4
REAL-WORLD DECISION-FOCUSED BENCHMARKS (PREDOPT)
To move beyond synthetic problems, we evaluate on three standard real-world tasks from the public
PREDOPT decision-focused-learning suite: Shortest Path (5↑5 grid LP, dy=40), Portfolio Op-
timization (Markowitz QP, dy=50), and Energy-Cost Scheduling (real 48-hour electricity prices,
dy=48). Table 6 and Figure 6 show OFP-SHADOW matches the exact CvxpyLayer normalized
regret on all three tasks (cosine 1.0000 vs. exact hypergradients) while being up to 2.6↑faster
than CvxpyLayer and 12.9↑faster than FFOCP in the backward pass, at a ﬂat memory footprint
(↓948 MB)—so the efﬁciency gains transfer to real-world DFL pipelines without loss in decision
quality.

Figure 8 | Qualitative comparison. Side-by-side comparison of the experiment section generated by
ScientistTwo against the highest-reviewed paper from ScientistOne (Meng et al., 2026).
Comparison with Human Researchers. We evaluate the research quality produced by Scien-
tistTwo against accepted publications. Specifically, we use ScholarPeer and the Stanford Agentic
Reviewer to evaluate papers accepted at NeurIPS 2025, ICLR 2026, and ICML 2026 (including
spotlight presentations), whose problem specifications and codebases serve as benchmark tasks for
ScientistTwo. As shown in Table 3, ScientistTwo successfully executes research on 86 out of 107
problems, achieving an 80.4% success rate. Furthermore, papers generated by ScientistTwo surpass
the average scores of accepted papers at ICLR 2026 and NeurIPS 2025 under both ScholarPeer and
Stanford Agentic Reviewer. While ScientistTwo does not yet achieve spotlight-level quality, these
results still demonstrate that it functions as an expert-level research agent capable of producing
manuscripts that meet the acceptance threshold of top-tier AI venues. Finally, we include comparisons
with AI-generated papers accepted at Agent4Science 2025—the first venue dedicated to AI-generated
research—to demonstrate that prior systems were incapable of meeting top conference standards.

Comparison with Human Researchers. We evaluate the research quality produced by Scien-
tistTwo against accepted publications. Specifically, we use ScholarPeer and the Stanford Agentic
Reviewer to evaluate papers accepted at NeurIPS 2025, ICLR 2026, and ICML 2026 (including
spotlight presentations), whose problem specifications and codebases serve as benchmark tasks for
ScientistTwo. As shown in Table 3, ScientistTwo successfully executes research on 86 out of 107
problems, achieving an 80.4% success rate. Furthermore, papers generated by ScientistTwo surpass
the average scores of accepted papers at ICLR 2026 and NeurIPS 2025 under both ScholarPeer and
Stanford Agentic Reviewer. While ScientistTwo does not yet achieve spotlight-level quality, these
results still demonstrate that it functions as an expert-level research agent capable of producing
manuscripts that meet the acceptance threshold of top-tier AI venues. Finally, we include comparisons
with AI-generated papers accepted at Agent4Science 2025—the first venue dedicated to AI-generated
research—to demonstrate that prior systems were incapable of meeting top conference standards.

blocks.text: ScientistTwo: Pioneering the Human Knowledge Frontier with Autonomous AI
• Round-Robin Placement (C0): A naive baseline that assigns models sequentially across

available GPUs in a cyclic order, completely ignoring memory capacities and SLO require-
ments.
• OpenEvolve (C1): An automated discovery framework based on AlphaEvolve that utilizes
evolutionary search to ﬁnd optimal placement conﬁgurations [Brown et al., 2025].
• AdaEvolve: An adaptive, LLM-driven zeroth-order optimization approach that iteratively
reﬁnes placements based on performance feedback [Cemri et al., 2026].
• EvoX: The current state-of-the-art meta-evolutionary search framework for automated
discovery, as reported in the benchmark leaderboard.

Evaluation Metrics
For this task, a higher score indicates a superior, more balanced model
placement.

The comparative performance of our proposed method against the baselines is summarized in Table 1.
Our Robust Multi-Heuristic Linearized Target Bisection method achieves a score of 26.2560. This
performance signiﬁcantly outperforms the naive Round-robin baseline, which completely fails to
optimize the objective, yielding a score of 0. Furthermore, our deterministic solver surpasses the
OpenEvolve framework, which achieves a score of 26.23.

While our method demonstrates strong performance, we note that it is highly competitive with,
but slightly trailing, AdaEvolve (26.30) and falls short of the unconstrained meta-evolutionary
search employed by EvoX (30.52). However, this performance delta highlights a crucial trade-off
between placement quality and computational overhead. Methods like AdaEvolve and EvoX rely on
heavy, LLM-driven zeroth-order optimization and meta-evolutionary loops, which require substantial
compute and time to converge.

In contrast, our proposed method is entirely deterministic and mathematically grounded in fractional
bin-packing principles [Alvim et al., 2004]. It achieves a 100% success rate in ﬁnding feasible place-
ments with an exceptionally low execution time of approximately 0.021 seconds. By transforming
the non-linear KVPR objective into a linearized capacity constraint, our solver rapidly explores the
search space using standard 1D bin-packing heuristics [Fekete and Schepers, 2001], making it highly
suitable for dynamic, real-time cluster orchestration where millisecond-level scheduling latency is
required.

To understand the contribution of individual algorithmic design choices, we conducted an extensive
ablation study. We evaluated several mathematical relaxations and search strategies that were explored
during the development of our solver. The results of this ablation are detailed in Table 2.

systematically evaluates O(1) model moves and swaps from the bottleneck GPU. By incrementally
updating precomputed state arrays, this reﬁnement irons out residual heuristic imperfections without
inﬂating execution time, proving to be a critical "ﬁnisher" for the algorithm.

Linearization vs. Iterative Reassignment
We also explored alternative mathematical approaches
to handle the fractional KVPR objective. An Iterative Dinkelbach-style Reassignment approach
achieved a score of 26.1906, while a pure Fractional Optimization via Dinkelbach’s Iterative Lin-
earization scored 26.0157. Both approaches underperformed compared to our target bisection method.
The fractional nature of the objective W/(M →S) ↑K transforms perfectly into the linear constraint
W +K ·S ↑K ·M. Bisection over the target K allows the solver to leverage robust, globally-aware
bin-packing heuristics rather than relying on iterative, gradient-like reassignments that are prone to
local optima in heavily constrained spaces.

Failure of Clustering-Based Heuristics
Finally, we tested clustering-inspired heuristics, including
Lloyd-Max Iterative Reassignment (score: 25.9551) and Complementary Workload-Aware Model
Pairing (score: 25.8152). These methods attempt to balance the mean KVPR or pair complementary
models prior to placement. However, they consistently failed to tightly pack the 80GB bins compared
to capacity-linearized bisection. The strictness of the memory constraint dictates that optimizing
for capacity utilization is a prerequisite for optimizing the fractional objective; clustering methods

inherently struggle to guarantee tight bin packings, leading to premature memory exhaustion and
sub-optimal maximum KVPR bounds.

In this work, we addressed the critical challenge of minimizing Key-Value Cache Pressure (KVPR)
in multi-tenant Large Language Model (LLM) serving environments. By formulating the model
placement task as a strict non-linear fractional bin-packing problem, we introduced a deterministic,
three-phase algorithmic pipeline comprising greedy initialization, multi-heuristic linearized target
bisection, and local search reﬁnement. Our approach effectively transforms the non-linear KVPR
objective into a solvable 1D capacity constraint. Experimental results demonstrate that our method
achieves a highly competitive KVPR score of 26.2560, outperforming sophisticated meta-evolutionary
frameworks such as OpenEvolve [Brown et al., 2025] and AdaEvolve [Cemri et al., 2026] while
maintaining a negligible computational overhead of approximately 0.021 seconds.

Despite these strong empirical results, our approach has several limitations. First, our solver assumes
a static, upfront placement of models based on proﬁled request rates and Service Level Objectives
(SLOs). In highly dynamic production environments where workload patterns ﬂuctuate unpredictably,
static placement may eventually lead to suboptimal resource utilization. Unlike systems that employ
dynamic execution-level chunking [Agrawal et al., 2023] or live migration of KV cache states [He
et al., 2025], our method does not currently adapt to real-time trafﬁc shifts after the initial placement.
Second, our formulation assumes a uniform 80GB memory constraint across all GPUs. While this
reﬂects standard high-end accelerator deployments, it does not account for heterogeneous clusters
with mixed memory capacities or complex network topologies, which have been explored in recent
systems like Helix [Mei et al., 2024] and DisHelis [Zhang et al., 2026]. Finally, our model abstracts
GPU memory as a contiguous pool, relying on the assumption that underlying systems handle
memory fragmentation effectively through techniques like virtual memory stitching or dynamic
paging [Prabhu et al., 2024].

Future research should explore extending our linearized bisection framework to online, dynamic
serving scenarios. Integrating our placement algorithm with proactive live migration mechanisms
could allow the system to continuously rebalance KVPR as request rates deviate from initial estimates

Comparison with AutoSOTA. While AutoSOTA (Li et al., 2026d) operates in a distinct setting, i.e.,
modifying existing codebases to optimize a single scalar metric, ScientistTwo is designed for end-to-
end scientific paper generation. For completeness, we provide a comparison based on the performance
gains reported over human state-of-the-art baselines. To extract these gains systematically, we parse
the main tables for 10 times using Gemini 3.6 Flash and averaged them. As shown in Table 4,
ScientistTwo shows superior performance to AutoSOTA in terms of average and median improvement
across average of all tasks and NeurIPS 2025 tasks, but performance drops slightly in the ICLR 2026
tasks. We hypothesize that this advantage stems from ScientistTwo proposing novel methodological
innovations to overcome baseline limitations, whereas AutoSOTA relies primarily on searching within
the existing hyperparameter and execution space to improve the given method. Appendix B examines
the five ICLR 2026 papers one by one and supports this account: none of AutoSOTA’s five changes
introduces a new algorithmic component, and each is a configuration-level edit of at most a few lines.

Balancing Exploration and Exploitation. As shown in Figure 9(b), the majority of the top-performing
ideas chosen by the Selector Agent are identified in the early stages. This indicates that the initial
seed ideas generated by ScientistTwo to overcome the limitations of human state-of-the-art methods
are already well-formed and competitive. Conversely, when seed ideas yield marginal gains or fail,
the Idea Evolver Agent leverages these experimental traces to evolve them into stronger hypotheses
that overcome baseline shortcomings. Consequently, as refinement progresses, newly selected best
ideas are substantially more likely to be drawn from evolved candidates rather than original seed
ideas (as evidenced by the dominant share of the blue bars after the initial round).
Effectiveness of the Rebuttal Agent. During the simulated dynamic peer-review phase, Scien-
tistTwo leverages the Rebuttal Agent to conduct supplementary experiments and uses the findings to
enhance the draft. As shown in Table 5, this rebuttal procedure effectively addresses the weaknesses
flagged by ScholarPeer. While it is not surprising that ScientistTwo gradually achieves good scores on
ScholarPeer, as we utilize ScholarPeer reviews, we found that our peer-review simulation framework
is generalized across Review Agent. Specifically, incorporating ScholarPeer reviews also improves
acceptance rate from Stanford Agentic Reviewer, with this effect being particularly pronounced in
the first review round. Furthermore, the first and second rows of Table 5 demonstrate that even
without the Rebuttal Agent, ScientistTwo produces initial drafts of significantly higher quality than the
prior state-of-the-art baseline, ScientistOne. This indicates that the preceding autonomous research
cycle—specifically the holistic benchmark reasoning, idea refinement, and ablation-driven hypothesis
refinement—is highly effective for drafting a robust manuscript, achieving a nearly 50% acceptance
rate when evaluated by both ScholarPeer and Stanford Agentic Reviewer.

that overcome baseline shortcomings. Consequently, as refinement progresses, newly selected best
ideas are substantially more likely to be drawn from evolved candidates rather than original seed
ideas (as evidenced by the dominant share of the blue bars after the initial round).

Effectiveness of the Rebuttal Agent. During the simulated dynamic peer-review phase, Scien-
tistTwo leverages the Rebuttal Agent to conduct supplementary experiments and uses the findings to
enhance the draft. As shown in Table 5, this rebuttal procedure effectively addresses the weaknesses
flagged by ScholarPeer. While it is not surprising that ScientistTwo gradually achieves good scores on
ScholarPeer, as we utilize ScholarPeer reviews, we found that our peer-review simulation framework
is generalized across Review Agent. Specifically, incorporating ScholarPeer reviews also improves
acceptance rate from Stanford Agentic Reviewer, with this effect being particularly pronounced in
the first review round. Furthermore, the first and second rows of Table 5 demonstrate that even
without the Rebuttal Agent, ScientistTwo produces initial drafts of significantly higher quality than the
prior state-of-the-art baseline, ScientistOne. This indicates that the preceding autonomous research
cycle—specifically the holistic benchmark reasoning, idea refinement, and ablation-driven hypothesis
refinement—is highly effective for drafting a robust manuscript, achieving a nearly 50% acceptance
rate when evaluated by both ScholarPeer and Stanford Agentic Reviewer.

Effectiveness of Review-Driven Idea Refinement. In the final stage, ScientistTwo employs the Meta-
Review Agent to evaluate whether the generated paper meets the acceptance standards of a top-tier
venue. If the agent indicates that further improvement is required, ScientistTwo refines the underlying
idea by incorporating the review as feedback. As shown in Table 6, this refinement process enables
ScientistTwo to generate more effective ideas that advance beyond the current knowledge frontier. For
instance, prior to review-driven refinement, ScientistTwo already established a new state-of-the-art
method, LFR-Engram, outperforming the human baseline Engram (Kwon et al., 2026). However,
the Meta-Review Agent deemed LFR-Engram insufficient to meet expert standards. By leveraging
the reviewer feedback for refinement, ScientistTwo subsequently synthesized FCD-Engram, which
consistently outperforms LFR-Engram. This case study demonstrates that review-driven refinement is
essential for producing more novel, high-impact research ideas.
CoE Integrity Audit. The CoE Integrity Audit (Meng et al., 2026) is a post-hoc evaluation framework
that verifies whether claims in a generated paper are supported by its artifacts: code, empirical
outputs, and bibliography. It comprises four integrity checks: (1) Score verification, which evaluates
codebase reproducibility by comparing reported scores against those obtained from re-executing the
repository; (2) Specification compliance, which ensures that solution code adheres strictly to task rules
without reward hacking; (3) Reference verification, which guarantees that the bibliography contains
no hallucinated citations; and (4) Method-code alignment, which ensures that the paper faithfully
and accurately describes the codebase implementation. Following Meng et al. (2026), AI-generated
papers and their corresponding codebases must be rigorously verifiable across all four dimensions.
To guarantee these properties, we introduce three dedicated refinement agents alongside careful
agent prompt design. For score verification, the Coding Agent is prompted during the experimen-
tation phase to output self-contained, reproducible scripts and execution instructions, ensuring full
reproducibility without requiring additional post-hoc refinement. For specification compliance, we
introduce a validation filter that uses the Coding Agent to detect and discard rule-violating solutions
immediately after experimentation. For reference verification, a search-augmented LLM identifies
